title: Cirrhosis: ascites, infection, encephalopathy, and what to avoid

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on AASLD practice guidance on ascites, hepatic encephalopathy and portal hypertension. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: A patient with cirrhosis is admitted with ascites. What is done to the ascites on admission?
questions.why: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is often silent, and a cell count on admission is how it is found. Coagulopathy is not a contraindication to the tap.

questions.q: What serum-ascites albumin gradient indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites?
questions.why: A gradient under 1.1 points to peritoneal causes such as malignancy, tuberculosis or pancreatitis, and to nephrotic syndrome.

questions.q: What ascitic fluid neutrophil count diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
questions.why: Treatment starts on the cell count, not the culture, with a third-generation cephalosporin. Cultures are negative in a large share of true cases.

questions.q: In spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, what does intravenous albumin on days 1 and 3 prevent?
questions.why: The doses are 1.5 g per kg on day 1 and 1 g per kg on day 3, given to patients with a creatinine over 1, urea over 30, or bilirubin over 4.

questions.q: Which patients with cirrhosis should be on antibiotic prophylaxis against spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
a: Anyone who has had an episode
Patients with an acute gastrointestinal bleed
Ascitic protein under 1.5 g/dL with kidney or liver dysfunction
d: Every patient on a transplant list
Patients with varices but no ascites
questions.why: Secondary prophylaxis is lifelong or until transplant. For a bleed it is seven days of ceftriaxone, whether or not there is ascites.

questions.q: What is the standard diuretic regimen for cirrhotic ascites?
questions.a: Spironolactone and furosemide together in a 100 to 40 ratio
questions.why: The ratio keeps potassium in balance. Sodium restriction to about 2 g a day comes first, and the doses step up together every few days to a maximum of 400 and 160.

questions.q: After a large-volume paracentesis of more than 5 litres, how much albumin is given per litre removed?
questions.why: Without it, post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction causes kidney injury and hyponatremia. Below 5 litres albumin is optional.

questions.q: What is first-line treatment for an episode of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.a: Lactulose titrated to two or three soft stools a day, and a search for the precipitant
questions.why: Infection, bleeding, constipation, dehydration, and sedatives are the usual precipitants. Rifaximin is added to prevent recurrence, and protein is not restricted.

questions.q: Which drug is preferred for primary prevention of variceal bleeding?
questions.why: A nonselective beta blocker lowers portal pressure; carvedilol does so more than propranolol or nadolol. Band ligation is the alternative for large varices when beta blockers are not tolerated.

questions.q: Which drugs should be avoided in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites?
d: Acetaminophen up to 2 g a day
questions.why: NSAIDs and renin-angiotensin blockers precipitate kidney injury and blunt diuretics. Acetaminophen in modest doses is the safest analgesic there is for these patients.

questions.q: How often should patients with cirrhosis have surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.why: Ultrasound, with or without alpha-fetoprotein. Any nodule over 1 cm goes on to a multiphase CT or MRI.

questions.q: At what MELD score should a patient be referred for transplant evaluation?
questions.why: Also with any decompensating event: ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy, or hepatocellular carcinoma. Referral is earlier than most people expect.
